title: The Approved-Only Model

scenario.situation: The risk team trained a default prediction model on 18 months of approved-loan outcomes. Backtest AUC is 0.82 and the team is ready to deploy it as the new application scorecard.
scenario.stakeholderBelief: The team assumes the model generalizes to all applicants — approved and would-be-rejected alike — because its backtest accuracy looks strong.
scenario.question: Is the model actually ready to score the full applicant population?

decisions.prompt: The team is eager to deploy. How do you frame your investigation before signing off?

options.label: Re-run the backtest on a held-out approved-loan sample
options.detail: Split the approved-loan data 80/20 and validate AUC on the holdout.
options.consequence: The holdout AUC is still 0.82 — reassuring, but the holdout was drawn from the same approved population. You've confirmed the model describes past approvals, not that it generalizes to rejections.
options.divergenceCost: Validated within the same biased sample — confirmed the bubble, not the blind spot.

options.label: Audit the training population against the full applicant population
options.detail: Compare the distribution of approved-loan borrowers to the broader applicant pool to check for selection bias.
options.consequence: You immediately see that approved borrowers occupy only the lower-risk tail of the applicant distribution. The model has never seen outcomes for higher-risk applicants, so its score surface is blind to that region.

options.label: Check model calibration on recent approvals
options.detail: Plot predicted vs. actual default rates on the most recent quarter of approved loans.
options.consequence: Calibration looks fine on approved loans — of course it does. You've checked the model on the only population it was trained on, leaving the survivorship gap completely unexamined.
options.divergenceCost: Checked calibration inside the survivors-only window and missed the unobserved population entirely.

options.label: Feature-importance audit for regulatory fairness
options.detail: Review which features drive scores to flag any proxies for protected classes.
options.consequence: Important for compliance, but this audit won't surface survivorship bias — a model can be feature-fair and still catastrophically wrong on the rejected population.
options.divergenceCost: Solved a real but separate problem while leaving the core generalization failure untouched.

decisions.prompt: You compare approved borrowers to the full applicant pool. Which metric best exposes the survivorship gap?

artifact.title: Applicant volume by model score decile — approved loans only
artifact.caption: Training records by score decile. Looks populated — but is this the full applicant picture?

options.label: Model AUC on approved-loan backtest
options.detail: Use the 0.82 AUC figure from the standard backtest as the performance benchmark.
options.consequence: AUC of 0.82 only measures rank-ordering within approved borrowers — people the old policy already filtered. It says nothing about how the model ranks applicants who would have been rejected.
options.divergenceCost: Accepted an AUC that measures discrimination inside the survivors, not across all applicants.

options.label: Approval rate (labelled outcomes) vs. total applicant volume by score decile
options.detail: For each score decile, compare how many total applicants applied versus how many have an observed outcome label.
options.consequence: The normalized view is stark: low-score deciles have near-zero label coverage — up to 94% of applicants in those deciles were rejected and carry no outcome. The model was never trained on the population it now has to score.

artifact.title: Label coverage rate by score decile (labelled approvals ÷ total applicants)
artifact.caption: In the lowest-score decile, only 6% of applicants have an observed outcome. The model has almost no signal about this population — yet deployment would score them.

decisions.prompt: Low-score deciles have near-zero label coverage, confirming the survivorship gap. What do you tell the team?

options.label: "The model is biased — reject it and retrain from scratch."
options.detail: Call the model unfit and block deployment.
options.consequence: You've correctly identified survivorship bias but overstepped into a prescriptive call without a validated fix. Reject inference techniques may recover the model; scrapping it entirely could waste 18 months of work and delay lending unnecessarily.
options.divergenceCost: Overclaimed the remedy — blocking deployment without evaluating whether reject inference could rehabilitate the model.

options.label: "The backtest flatters the model — it was trained only on survivors. Before deploying on all applicants, we need reject inference or a shadow period to estimate outcomes for the unobserved population."
options.detail: Present the survivorship finding and recommend a concrete path to a valid model.
options.consequence: The team now understands why 0.82 AUC does not mean 'ready to deploy everywhere.' You've reframed the problem, quantified the gap, and handed them a concrete remediation path — reject inference augmentation or a controlled shadow deployment — without overclaiming what the data can prove.

insight: A model trained only on approved loans achieves high backtest AUC because it is evaluated on the very population it learned from — the low-risk survivors of a prior acceptance policy. When deployed as a full applicant scorecard, it scores a large unobserved population (historic rejects) with almost no calibrating signal, systematically mis-ranking them. The lesson is survivorship bias in supervised learning: the label you can observe is not a random sample of the label you need, and AUC within the observed set is not evidence of generalization across the full input space. The fix — reject inference — imputes or estimates outcomes for the unlabelled population before retraining.
